item.title: Extracting ICD-10 Code list using R and the WHO ICD API
item.description:
From the WHO ICD-10 browser to a tidy, analysis-ready dataset

Introduction

If you work with health data, sooner or later you will meet the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, better known as ICD. It is the global standard, maintained by the World Health Organization (WHO), for recording diagnoses and causes of death.

The tenth revision, ICD-10, was endorsed by the World Health Assembly in May 1990 and has been in use in WHO member states since 1993 WHO adopted ICD-11 in 2019, and it came into effect in January 2022, but moving a whole health system to a new classification takes years. ICD-10 is still the version behind most hospital records, death registers, insurance claims and research databases around the world, and it will be for a while yet.

WHO publishes the 2019 edition of ICD-10 in an online browser at icd.who.int/browse10/2019/en. The browser is great for looking up a single code. It is much less helpful when you need all of them in a spreadsheet or a data frame, because there is no button to export the full list.

In this post, I show how I extracted the complete ICD-10 code list, with each code’s block and chapter, using R and the free WHO ICD API. The final script fetches 12,301 codes in under a minute.

Why you would want the full code list

Diagnosis codes rarely arrive with their meaning attached. A hospital extract might give you a column like primary_dx containing A09, J18.9 or O80, and nothing else. To do almost anything useful with it, you need a lookup table that tells you what each code means and where it sits in the classification. Some common uses:

  • Defining study outcomes. Many studies define their outcomes from diagnosis codes, for example “any hospital admission for pneumonia” or “death from a cardiovascular cause”. That means listing every code that belongs to the outcome, often whole blocks or chapters.
  • Grouping diagnoses. Thousands of individual codes are hard to analyse. The ICD hierarchy groups them into 22 chapters and a few hundred blocks, so you can summarise admissions or deaths by body system or disease group.
  • Comorbidity scores. Widely used indices such as Charlson and Elixhauser are defined as lists of ICD-10 codes.
  • Labelling and checking data. Joining a lookup table to your data turns B54 into “Unspecified malaria” in tables and figures. It also flags invalid or mistyped codes, because they won’t match.
  • Mapping to other systems. Translating codes between classifications, or from free-text diagnoses to codes, needs a complete reference list to map against.

The problem with copy and paste

The obvious approach is to open the browser and copy the codes into Excel. That was my first attempt too: I copied the block headings, chapter by chapter, into a spreadsheet. It works for a handful of codes, but for the full list it has real problems:

  • It is slow. ICD-10 has 22 chapters, 263 blocks and more than 12,000 codes once you include the subcategories (the codes with a decimal point, such as A00.1). Expanding and copying every branch of the tree by hand takes days.
  • It is error-prone. It is very easy to skip a block, paste a row twice or truncate a long title. When I later compared my hand-made list with the API version, whole chapters were missing: pregnancy (O codes), perinatal conditions (P), congenital malformations (Q), health status (Z) and special purposes (U).
  • It is hard to repeat. WHO updates the classification, and nobody wants to redo days of copying. A script can be rerun in a minute.
  • It leaves no record. A spreadsheet doesn’t show where the data came from or how it was put together. A script documents exactly how the dataset was built, which matters for reproducible research.

A programmatic extract fixes all four. The same code gives the same complete dataset every time, for anyone who runs it, anywhere in the world.

The WHO ICD API

Behind the browser, WHO provides the ICD API, a free web service that returns the classification as JSON. It covers both ICD-11 and ICD-10. For ICD-10, every chapter, block and code has its own address:

https://id.who.int/icd/release/10/2019            the 2019 release
https://id.who.int/icd/release/10/2019/I          chapter I
https://id.who.int/icd/release/10/2019/A00-A09    a block
https://id.who.int/icd/release/10/2019/A00        a three-character code
https://id.who.int/icd/release/10/2019/A00.0      a subcategory

Each response contains the entity’s title and, most usefully, a list of its children. Ask for the 2019 release and you get the 22 chapters. Ask for a chapter and you get its blocks. Ask for a block and you get its codes, and so on. This means we don’t have to guess which codes exist: we start at the top and follow the tree down.

Getting API access

To use the API:

  1. Register for a free account at icd.who.int/icdapi.
  2. Open View API access key(s) to get your Client ID and Client Secret.
  3. Save them in your ~/.Renviron file, so they never appear in your scripts, and restart R:
icd_client_id=your-client-id
icd_client_secret=your-client-secret

The API uses OAuth2 client credentials. You exchange the ID and secret for an access token, which is valid for one hour. You could paste a token into your script, but it will expire, and a long run will start failing partway through. It’s better to let R request and renew the token for you, as shown below.

Extracting the codes in R

Every code block in this section runs as written. Copy them into a script, or download this post’s index.qmd and render it, and you will get the same dataset, table and chart you see below. The only thing you need is your own API credentials in ~/.Renviron, as described above.

Note

The outputs on this page were produced by running the code when the post was rendered. Your numbers will match as long as WHO has not changed the 2019 release.

The code uses {httr2} for the API requests, {tidyverse} for data wrangling, {rio} to export the result and {DT} for the interactive table.

# install any missing packages, then load them all
pacman::p_load(
  httr2,      # build and send the API requests
  tidyverse,  # data wrangling: dplyr, tidyr, stringr, purrr, ggplot2
  rio,        # export the final dataset to Excel
  DT          # interactive table of the results
)

1. Authentication that renews itself

{httr2} has built-in OAuth support. We describe the WHO token endpoint once, and every request then gets a valid token automatically. It is fetched on first use, cached, and renewed when it expires.

# read the API credentials saved in ~/.Renviron (never type them in the code)
icd_client_id     <- Sys.getenv("icd_client_id")
icd_client_secret <- Sys.getenv("icd_client_secret")

# stop early with a clear message if the credentials are missing
if (!nzchar(icd_client_id) || !nzchar(icd_client_secret)) {
  stop("Set icd_client_id and icd_client_secret in ~/.Renviron, then restart R")
}

# describe the WHO token endpoint; httr2 fetches, caches and renews the token
icd_client <- oauth_client(
  id        = icd_client_id,
  secret    = icd_client_secret,
  token_url = "https://icdaccessmanagement.who.int/connect/token",
  name      = "who_icd_api"
)

# the ICD-10 release to extract, and the address at the top of its tree
icd_release <- "2019"
icd_root    <- str_glue("https://id.who.int/icd/release/10/{icd_release}")

# number of requests sent to the API at the same time
n_parallel  <- 10

2. One function to build every request

Every request needs the same headers, authentication and error handling, so we wrap them in a small function. Two details matter a lot for a run of more than 12,000 requests:

  • Retries. Servers sometimes answer “too many requests” (HTTP 429) or have a temporary hiccup (5xx errors). req_retry() waits and tries again instead of giving up. retry_on_failure = TRUE also retries when the connection drops altogether.
  • HTTP/1.1. With many parallel requests, I saw the server reset connections with the error Error in the HTTP2 framing layer. Using the older HTTP/1.1 protocol made those errors go away.
# the API returns http:// links, request them over https
to_https <- \(x) str_replace(x, "^http://", "https://")

# build (but don't send) the request for one API address
icd_request <- function(url) {
  request(url) |>
    # ask for JSON, API version 2 and English titles
    req_headers(
      accept = "application/json",
      `API-Version` = "v2",
      `Accept-Language` = "en"
    ) |>
    # retry rate limits, server errors and dropped connections, waiting longer each time
    req_retry(
      max_tries = 5,
      retry_on_failure = TRUE,
      is_transient = \(resp) resp_status(resp) %in% c(429, 500, 502, 503, 504)
    ) |>
    # use HTTP/1.1 (curl's code 2) to avoid HTTP/2 resets under parallel load
    req_options(http_version = 2) |>
    # give up on a single attempt after 60 seconds (it is then retried)
    req_timeout(60) |>
    # log in with OAuth; the token is fetched and renewed automatically
    req_oauth_client_credentials(icd_client, scope = "icdapi_access")
}

3. Fetching many entities in parallel

Sending requests one at a time is the main reason scripts like this are slow. req_perform_parallel() keeps several requests in flight at once. With on_error = "continue", one failure doesn’t stop the batch; we get the error back and decide what to do with it.

That decision is important. My first version caught every error and treated it as “this code doesn’t exist”. When the token expired, every request after that failed, and the codes silently disappeared from the output. Here, failures are kept in their own table, and an authentication error (HTTP 401) stops the run straight away with a clear message.

# request many addresses in parallel; return the results and failures separately
fetch_entities <- function(urls) {
  # send up to n_parallel requests at once; keep going if some fail.
  # The progress bar only shows when running interactively, not when rendering
  resps <- map(urls, icd_request) |>
    req_perform_parallel(on_error = "continue", max_active = n_parallel,
                         progress = interactive())

  # TRUE for requests that got a response, FALSE for those that failed
  ok <- map_lgl(resps, \(r) inherits(r, "httr2_response"))

  # one row per failed request: its address, HTTP status (if any) and error message
  failed <- tibble(
    url     = urls[!ok],
    status  = map_int(resps[!ok], \(e) if (inherits(e, "httr2_http"))
                                         resp_status(e$resp) else NA_integer_),
    message = map_chr(resps[!ok], conditionMessage)
  )

  # an expired or invalid token makes every remaining request fail, so stop here
  if (any(failed$status %in% 401)) {
    stop("ICD API returned 401 (unauthorised): token expired or credentials invalid")
  }

  # turn each successful response into a one-row table, then stack them
  parsed <- map(resps[ok], \(r) {
    json <- resp_body_json(r)
    tibble(
      api_url    = to_https(json$`@id`),                         # entity address
      code_label = json$title$`@value` %||% NA_character_,       # English title
      child_urls = list(to_https(as.character(unlist(json$child))))  # its children
    )
  }) |>
    bind_rows()

  list(ok = ok, parsed = parsed, failed = failed)
}

4. Walking down the tree

Now we start at the 2019 release and work down one level at a time. Each level’s children become the next level’s requests, until we reach codes that have no children.

As we go, each entity passes its chapter and block down to its children. Once we reach a code, we already know which block and chapter it belongs to, so we don’t need a separate lookup table. Some chapters have nested blocks (for example, C00-C97 contains C00-C75, which contains C00-C14), and each code is assigned to its most specific block.

start_time <- Sys.time()

# request the top of the tree; its children are the 22 chapters
root_resp    <- icd_request(icd_root) |> req_perform()
chapter_urls <- to_https(as.character(unlist(resp_body_json(root_resp)$child)))

# the queue holds the entities still to request, with what they inherit from above
queue <- tibble(
  url            = chapter_urls,
  parent_url     = as.character(icd_root),
  chapter        = NA_character_,
  chapter_topic  = NA_character_,
  category_code  = NA_character_,
  category_topic = NA_character_
)

# collect each level's results and failures in lists, combine once at the end
levels_list <- list()
failed_list <- list()
depth       <- 1

# keep going until a level has no children left to request
while (nrow(queue) > 0) {
  message(str_glue("Level {depth}: requesting {nrow(queue)} entities"))

  res <- fetch_entities(queue$url)
  failed_list[[depth]] <- res$failed

  # put the inherited columns next to the new results (same row order)
  level_df <- bind_cols(select(queue[res$ok, ], -url), res$parsed) |>
    mutate(
      level          = depth,
      icd_code       = str_extract(api_url, "[^/]+$"),          # text after the last /
      is_block       = str_detect(icd_code, "-"),               # blocks look like A00-A09
      chapter        = if (depth == 1) icd_code else chapter,   # level 1 rows are chapters
      chapter_topic  = if (depth == 1) code_label else chapter_topic,
      category_code  = if_else(is_block, icd_code, category_code),   # nearest block
      category_topic = if_else(is_block, code_label, category_topic)
    )

  levels_list[[depth]] <- level_df

  # the children of this level become the next queue, one row per child
  queue <- level_df |>
    select(parent_url = api_url, url = child_urls,
           chapter, chapter_topic, category_code, category_topic) |>
    unnest(url)

  depth <- depth + 1
}
Level 1: requesting 22 entities
Level 2: requesting 211 entities
Level 3: requesting 1660 entities
Level 4: requesting 8254 entities
Level 5: requesting 1340 entities
Level 6: requesting 1110 entities
# combine all levels, and all failures
icd10_entities <- bind_rows(levels_list)
icd10_failed   <- bind_rows(failed_list)

# report failures loudly instead of dropping them silently
if (nrow(icd10_failed) > 0) {
  warning(str_glue("{nrow(icd10_failed)} requests failed after retries"))
}

elapsed <- difftime(Sys.time(), start_time, units = "secs")

The messages above show the progress through the tree. This run took 59 seconds, with 0 failed requests.

5. The final dataset

Finally, we drop the chapter and block rows, keep the codes, and add a link to each code’s page in the WHO browser. That link is handy when someone wants to read the full inclusion and exclusion notes for a code.

icd10_codes <- icd10_entities |>
  # keep the codes: drop chapters (level 1) and blocks
  filter(level > 1, !is_block) |>
  # choose and order the final columns
  transmute(
    icd_code,
    code_label,
    icd_code_api_url    = api_url,
    icd_code_direct_url = str_glue("https://icd.who.int/browse10/{icd_release}/en#/{icd_code}"),
    category_code,
    category_topic,
    chapter,
    chapter_topic
  ) |>
  # sort in code order: A00, A00.0, A00.1, ..., A01
  arrange(icd_code)

# export the codes, plus any failed requests so nothing goes missing unnoticed.
# The file is saved in the working directory
list(icd10_codes = icd10_codes, failed_requests = icd10_failed) |>
  export("datasets/2019_icd10_codes.xlsx")

The result is one tidy row per code. The full dataset is saved to Excel; to keep this page light, the table below shows only two chapters, both major causes of death and illness worldwide: chapter I, infectious and parasitic diseases such as malaria, tuberculosis and diarrhoeal disease, and chapter II, neoplasms (cancers). Search the table, or filter any column. Each code links to its page in the WHO browser.

# chapters covering many of the most common diseases worldwide
common_chapters <- c("I", "II")

icd10_codes |>
  # show only those chapters, to keep the page light
  filter(chapter %in% common_chapters) |>
  # turn each code into a link to its page in the WHO ICD-10 browser
  mutate(icd_code = str_glue('<a href="{icd_code_direct_url}" target="_blank">{icd_code}</a>')) |>
  select(icd_code, code_label, category_code, category_topic, chapter, chapter_topic) |>
  datatable(
    rownames = FALSE,
    class    = "compact stripe hover",
    colnames = c("Code", "Title", "Block", "Block title", "Chapter", "Chapter title"),
    filter   = "top",                                     # a filter box above each column
    escape   = -1,                                        # escape all but column 1, so the code links stay clickable
    options  = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE)
  )

In total, the dataset has 12,301 codes: 2,090 three-character codes plus their subcategories, across 22 chapters and 263 blocks.

# chapters in their natural order (I to XXII), not alphabetical
chapter_order <- as.character(as.roman(1:22))

icd10_codes |>
  count(chapter, chapter_topic) |>
  mutate(
    chapter = factor(chapter, levels = chapter_order),
    label   = str_c(chapter, "  ", str_trunc(chapter_topic, 48))
  ) |>
  arrange(chapter) |>
  # chapter I at the top of the chart
  mutate(label = fct_rev(fct_inorder(label))) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, label)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a78d6", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = format(n, big.mark = ",")), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank())

Using the dataset

With the lookup table in hand, labelling and grouping diagnosis data takes a single join. To show how, here is a small made-up admissions dataset, with the kind of messy codes you see in real data:

# made-up admissions: note the lower case, the trailing space and the invalid K99
admissions <- tibble(
  patient_id = 1:8,
  primary_dx = c("A09", "j18.9", "B54", "J18.9 ", "E43", "A09", "K99", "I21.9")
)

# tidy the codes, then join the lookup table to label them
admissions_labelled <- admissions |>
  mutate(icd_code = str_trim(toupper(primary_dx))) |>
  left_join(icd10_codes, by = "icd_code")

# count admissions by chapter
admissions_labelled |>
  count(chapter, chapter_topic, sort = TRUE)
# A tibble: 5 × 3
  chapter chapter_topic                                     n
  <chr>   <chr>                                         <int>
1 I       Certain infectious and parasitic diseases         3
2 X       Diseases of the respiratory system                2
3 IV      Endocrine, nutritional and metabolic diseases     1
4 IX      Diseases of the circulatory system                1
5 <NA>    <NA>                                              1

Any code that finds no match after the join is a good candidate for a data query:

# codes that are not in the WHO ICD-10 list
admissions_labelled |>
  filter(is.na(code_label)) |>
  select(patient_id, primary_dx)
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  patient_id primary_dx
       <int> <chr>     
1          7 K99

Defining an outcome from whole blocks becomes a filter rather than a hand-typed list of codes:

# all codes in the "Influenza and pneumonia" block, J09-J18
pneumonia_codes <- icd10_codes |>
  filter(category_code == "J09-J18") |>
  pull(icd_code)

length(pneumonia_codes)
[1] 44
head(pneumonia_codes, 15)
 [1] "J09"   "J10"   "J10.0" "J10.1" "J10.8" "J11"   "J11.0" "J11.1" "J11.8"
[10] "J12"   "J12.0" "J12.1" "J12.2" "J12.3" "J12.8"

Speed and lessons learned

My first version of this script took about 30 minutes and, as it turned out, quietly missed thousands of codes. The final version takes under a minute and reports every failure. The main changes were:

  1. Follow the tree instead of guessing. The first version built candidate codes (A00.0 to A00.9 for every three-character code) and asked the API whether each one existed. Most of them don’t, so most requests were wasted. Following the API’s own child links requests only codes that exist, and it also finds codes with a fifth character, such as B18.00, that guessing would miss.
  2. Run requests in parallel. Ten requests in flight at once, instead of one, cut the waiting time dramatically.
  3. Never treat every error as “not found”. A missing code, an expired token and a dropped connection are different problems. Retry what is temporary, stop on authentication errors, and record the rest.
  4. Let the library manage the token. OAuth client credentials with {httr2} remove the one-hour token expiry problem entirely.
  5. Check the result against what you expect. Comparing the new output with my old hand-built list is how I found both the missing chapters and the duplicated rows in the old version.

A few caveats

  • This is the WHO version of ICD-10. Several countries use their own national modifications, such as ICD-10-CM in the United States, ICD-10-AM in Australia and ICD-10-GM in Germany. These add many codes that the WHO version doesn’t have. If your data use a national modification, get the code list from the organisation that maintains it.
  • Titles are not the whole story. Many codes come with inclusion and exclusion notes that matter for correct coding. The icd_code_direct_url column links to each code’s page in the browser so you can read them.
  • The same approach works for ICD-11. The API has the same tree structure for ICD-11, so the traversal can be adapted when you move to the new revision.

Conclusion

Copying ICD-10 codes by hand from a website is slow, error-prone and impossible to reproduce. With the free WHO ICD API and fewer than 200 lines of R, you can build a complete, well-structured ICD-10 lookup table in under a minute, and rebuild it whenever you need to.

For researchers working with routine health data anywhere in the world, that table is a foundation for defining outcomes, grouping diagnoses, computing comorbidity scores and checking data quality. I hope this saves you the days of copy and paste it would otherwise take.

item.title: Web scraping using R
item.description:
Efficient, flexible and powerful!

Introduction

Web scraping is concept that most probably you have heard about. This is the art of harvesting publicly available data from a website for use in your analysis or reporting. Web scraping can be as simple as copying the contents of a website and pasting them on an excel sheet, but that’s not what we are going to do today. Most website pages are built using HTML and this allows us to use tools such as R to dynamically extract the data.

In this tutorial, I am going walk you through how you can harvest data from websites using R programming language. You can do this by coding the logic and instructions manually or use the package {rvest} to easily extract the contents of a website. We would demonstrate the examples using the below two websites.

  • TheGlobalEconomy.com, Exchange rate to USD by country
  • CRAN package website and package download metrics website

First, let’s load the packages/tools of trade for the exercise.

# loading packages
pacman::p_load(
  rvest,        # functions for webscraping
  ggthemes,     # extend themes for ggplot2
  lubridate,    # handle dates
  here,         # manage file paths
  flextable,    # quick tables
  tidyverse     # data wranglinga and visualization
)

# set theme for ggplot2
theme_set(
  theme_hc(base_size = 18) +                  # base size
    theme(
      legend.position = "none",              # No legend, unless specified in the plot
      legend.title = element_blank(),         # No title on the legend
      axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 90) # spin y title 90 degrees
    )
)

using rvest

This is the simplest and easiest approach of then all. rvest helps you scrape (or harvest) data from web pages and it’s designed to work with the pipe chain style of coding.

Three simples steps using this package:-

  • Use read_tml function to convert the the url into an xml document
  • pass the xlm document to the function html_table to convert it into a list contain table(s) from the url source site.
  • Now that you have tabular data, you can proceed with various data wrangling approaches to clean it up for use.

Dollar exchange data

I came across this website Exchange rate to USD by country while I was working on aggregating output from aneconomic micro-simulation model estimating benefits and budget impact of setting up fracture liaison services. Part of my reporting costs associated with the FLS, reported in local currency for about 10 different countries, but for harmonized reporting and international consumption, I need to convert the local currencies to US Dollars, hence I needed a source that I could cite and is updated regularly.

# get url from website
exchange_rate_url <- "https://www.theglobaleconomy.com/rankings/Dollar_exchange_rate/"

# read HTML from website
exchange_rate_webpage <- read_html(exchange_rate_url)       # read html site


# create a datframe containing the exchange rates for use
currency_rates <- exchange_rate_webpage %>%
  html_table() %>%                                          # output a list contain the exchange rate table from website
  as.data.frame() %>%                                       # transform into a tibble
  # rename columns appropriately
  rename(
    Country        = Countries,
    DateLatestData     = "Reference",
    LatesValue     = "Latest.value",
    Change3months  = "Change.three.months",
    Change12months = "Change.twelve.months"
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(LatesValue, as.numeric),                  # convert to numeric column containing exchange rate
         
         # On the date column; remove white space and replace "/" with "-"
         DateLatestData = str_squish(
           str_replace_all(
             string = DateLatestData,
             pattern = "/",
             replacement = "-"
           )
         )) %>% 
  # transform `DateLatestData` into a proper date column
  mutate(
    DateLatestData = my(DateLatestData),                       # proper date format
    DateLatestData = format(DateLatestData, "%Y-%m")           # YYYY-mm
  )

You can now export the harvested data for later use downstream or in your modelling framework like I did. You see, easy and straight forward, right?

# Export the data

rio::export(currency_rates, here("datasets", "dollar_exchange_rates.rds"))

Available CRAN packages

In this section, we are going to harvest data from two websites:-

  • List of available CRAN packages by data of publication
  • Tracked website of CRAN packages by number of downloads
  • Additionally, to get some metrics to combine with data from the above 2 sites, we I use available.packages function for all cran packages in this mirror

CRAN packages by publication date

I will use the 3 simple steps already covered earlier, employing rvest package.

# Specifying the url

item.title: dplyr::coalesce() in action
item.description:
Viable shortcut to missing-value-free data set

Introduction

Missing data can be a major headache when handling data in R; more especially if these NA’s are scattered across multiple columns representing your one variable of interest.

The coalesce() function from dplyr package comes in handy in such situations. In this short article, I am going to show you how powerful the function coalesce() is and how it can make your data manipulation task easy. To put in perspective, the function extracts the first non-missing (non-NA) value from a set of columns or values, making your data cleaner and analysis-ready, it does this by prioritizing a designated column as we will see from the worked out examples below.

Create fictious data

# load packages
pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse,
  flextable
)

# Create fictitious data
fict_data <- tribble(
 ~PTID, ~ HT_ADM, ~ HT_DISCH, ~ HT_D45, ~ HT_D90,       # patient ID and Height measurements at different time-points
  "7001",    100,      100.1,        100,       NA_real_,
  "7002",    97,       98,         NA_real_,  97.5,
  "7003",    97.6,     NA_real_,    97,      97.5,
  "7004",    NA_real_,  99,        99.8,     100,
  "7005",    79.5,  NA_real_,   78.9,     NA_real_,
  "7006",    NA_real_,  NA_real_,   NA_real_,  102.1,
  "7007",    78.5,      79,         NA_real_,    NA_real_,
  "7008",    NA_real_,      98,        98,       NA_real_)
# qflextable-it
fict_data %>% 
  qflextable()

Creating Height column

The aim is to use coalesce() to create a column HT_cm with non-missing data using. We can try a few combination, but I am confident that if you look carefully, there are probably a few combination of two columns that can give you that.

item.title: Celebrating 100 days of Gym dedication
item.description:
Because I can exercise and share a brief story!

Introduction

Welcome to the journey of celebrating 100 days of unwavering dedication to my fitness regimen. Beginning of the year, I embarked on a quest for personal betterment, focusing on gym weight-lifting and outdoor running exercises, with a target of achieving at least 11 kilometers each weekend (fun fact: I exceeded my goal by running approximately 28 kilometers in just about two weekends).

This journey culminated in a staggering 100 days of sheer hard work, unwavering dedication, and a growing passion for all things fitness. In this article, I aim to take you through this transformative 100-day journey, sharing the challenges I overcame, and the invaluable lessons I’ve learned along the way.

# Load packages for session
pacman::p_load(
  lubridate,   # handle and manage dates
  flextable,   # for quick and neat tables
  ggthemes,    # ggplot2 themes extension
  here,        # manage file paths
  rio,         # data import
  scales,      # for the date label function
  tidyverse    # data wrangling and viz
)

# set theme for ggplot2
theme_set(
  theme_hc(base_size = 18) +                  # base size
    theme(
      legend.position = "none",              # No legend, unless specified in the plot
      legend.title = element_blank(),         # No title on the legend
      axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 90) # spin y title 90 degrees
    )
)

The below code below utilize the tribble function to create row-wise tibble of the workout data for the months beggining January 2023 to my celebration month and date.

I also import an excel log (from the gym logs) capturing start and end times for all the gym workouts for the months listed. This will be used to create interesting visualization later on.

# Creating tibble for monthly workout counts
# used to visualize in the latter sections
workout_df <- tribble(
  ~ month, ~n_workouts,
  "2023-01", 14 ,
  "2023-02", 13,
  "2023-03",05 ,
  "2023-04", 0,
  "2023-05",02 ,
  "2023-06",14 ,
  "2023-07", 23,
  "2023-08", 15,
  "2023-09",0 ,
  "2023-10", 14
)

# import gym logs
gym_log_raw <- import(here("posts","celebrate-100-gym-days", "chris-gym_game.xlsx"))

# data processing
workout_df <- workout_df %>% 
  mutate(
    month = ym(month),
    n_workouts = as.integer(n_workouts)
  )

Cleaning gym logs data

# clean the gym log data
gym_log <- gym_log_raw %>% 
  
  # create visit date, stat time and end time
  mutate(
    visit_start_time  = str_extract(visit_start, "\\d+:\\d+[aApP][mM]"),       # extract time component
    visit_end_time    = str_extract(visit_end, "\\d+:\\d+[aApP][mM]"),         # extract time component
    visit_date        = str_extract(visit_start, "\\d{2} [A-Za-z]{3} \\d{2}"), # extract date component
    visit_date        = dmy(visit_date),                                       # convert into ISO date
    week_day          = wday(visit_date, label = T, abbr = T),                 # day of the week
    month             = month(visit_date, label = T),                          # workout month
    duration_mins     = as.integer(str_remove(duration, " minutes")),          # minutes in the gym
    morning_wkout     = ifelse(str_detect(visit_start, "am"), "Yes", "No")     # Morning workout (Yes/No)
  ) %>% 
  
  # drop the first 3 columns, not neede downstream
  select(-c(1:3)) %>% 
  arrange(visit_date)

My journey commenced with setting realistic and achievable fitness goals, providing me with a clear path and unwavering focus. My objectives included:-

  • Enhancing full-body muscle strength
  • Build endurance
  • Overall fitness

My workout routine was marked by monthly fluctuations, and I visualized these trends to identify both my best and most challenging months.

workout_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = n_workouts, group = 1)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_workouts)) +   # size of point depends on number of workouts
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Trend of monthly gym workouts",
       subtitle = "Past 10 months only",

  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "month",    # break by 1 month interval

Figure 1 shows a trend of monthly workouts, with my worst efforts in the months of March and May (I have an excuse though 😂). I reached by best efforts in the month of July with a total of 23 gym works in that monthly only 😰, never managed to replicate that effort, it has now since become my other additional goal, you see how it works now?

workout_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = n_workouts, x = factor(1))) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2) +
  labs(title = "The overal picture",
       x = "", y = "No. of workouts") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())

I averaged 10 workouts per month during the 10 months period (despite registering 0 in April and May) Figure 2. I registered a median of 13 workouts per month, not bad for a beginner though, proud of these numbers to the greatest heights.

Monthly Visual Chart

The cascede images below shows monthly presence in the gym. The light-green highlighted dates represents the days I worked out for that month. July has a good pattern, I love it 🤗

Workout schedule: Structuring Success

A structured workout schedule was instrumental in maintaining consistency. It included various exercises targeting different muscle groups and allocated specific times to each.

# Work out schedule
workout_sched <- tribble(
  ~ Day, ~ `50 mins`, ~ `30 mins`, ~`10 mins`,
  "Monday", "Chest", "Biceps", "Treadmill Run",
  "Tuesday", "Back", "Triceps", "Treadmill Run",

  "Friday", NA_character_, NA_character_, "Rest day (Not always)",

As a starting point, I aimed at working out for at least 1hr 30 mins; focusing two muscles a day as shown in Table 1. Friday was not all rest day as can been seen in monthly visual chart - 3, but was mostly a plan to catch up on missed appointment a.k.a punish yourself for missing many sessions the prior month.

Visualizing Progress: Tracking Transformations

Visualizing my workout data unveiled the trends in my workout duration, enabling me to track improvements and shifts in my routine.

Average monthly workout duration

gym_log %>% 
  group_by(month) %>% 
  summarise(
    avg_dur = mean(duration_mins)
  ) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = avg_dur, group = 1)) +
  geom_line()+
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly average workout duration in minutes",
    x = "Month",
    y = "duration (mins)"
  )

The month of June was my worst solo effort, but this trend shows the significance of my gym buddy the month of after June and the average stay and working out in the gym that shot up by approximately 38% and almost stabilized. I can only hope for an upward trend going forward.

Trend - best month

The month after getting a workout buddy was the best. All metrics were at their all time best i.e. more days in the gym, more time working out for the days designated; and in fact, the second best monthly average workout duration this year Figure 3. This once again tells the importance of the incoming energy, support, encouragement and accountability from my workout buddy.

# create metrics for dynamic labeling
tot_mins <- gym_log %>% filter(month == "Jul") %>% 
  select(duration_mins) %>% pluck() %>% sum()

# days worked
days_work <- gym_log %>% filter(month == "Jul") %>% nrow()
 

gym_log %>% 
  filter(month == "Jul") %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = visit_date, y = duration_mins, group = 1)) + 
  geom_point()+
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 days",    # break by 1 month interval
               #date_labels = "%d\n%b",
               labels = label_date_short()) +       # show only month of the year
  labs(x = "Date", y = "duration(mins)",
       title = "Trend of best effort, July 2023",
       caption = str_glue("Days working out = {days_work}\nTotal mins = {comma(tot_mins)}"))

Summary of workout days:Evolution of Dedication

In general, my working out routine greatly improved months following June and this can all be attributed to having a workout buddy. The box plots below paint a picture of a transformation in the process; which can only get better with time. Amidst all the fired up effort, I missed a few days/months; but that’s a story for another day of why that happened.

gym_log %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = duration_mins)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.color = "red") +
  labs(y = "duration(mins)")

Summarizing my monthly workouts using box plots revealed the distribution of my workout durations and provided further insights into my fitness journey Figure 5.

Histogram of workout duration

A histogram of workout duration showcases the diverse nature of my exercise routines, with both short, intense sessions and longer, endurance-based workouts.

I am proud of every value on the x-axis and how many times it occurred on the y-axis. I don’t want to settle on the middle ground but I lik the extremes because they come into play when circumstance prevail.

gym_log %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = duration_mins)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "duration(mins)", y = "Frequency",
       title = "Histogram of all-time workout duration",
       subtitle = "Jan upto Oct 2023")

Conclusion and take aways

This celebration is about a habit I have managed to pick, the growth and the transformation it has brought about.This type of a journey requires accountability, and for that reason, I have a workout buddy Tony Henry who I am accountable to, and the gym app was very crucial in tracking my progress.

Fitness journey comes with challenges, for instance having to wake up in the morning at around 6am to workout while you would rather keep warm and sleep is the hardest choice. Overcoming this type of challenge was key to my success, made me mentally stronger and enabled me to become more resilient.

Listen to your body always, know when to push harder and when to rest. Celebrate every milestone you have achieved, even if it meant you lifted 2.5kg extra on top of your regular weight limit. Celebrations makes you more energetic and looking forward to move up next level the following workout day.

I hope my story inspires you to start your fitness journey or continue the one you already archived. It’s doable, if you put mind to it. Here is to 100 days of hard-work, dedication and determination 🙌🥳.

item.description:
MySQL, SQLite, R

This blog post comes as a follow-up to a successful online training session jointly organized by NairobiR and RLadies on June 12, 2021. If you missed the session, you can view the recording on this YouTube link

In both the video and this accompanying blog, I delve into the fundamental principles of establishing dynamic connections and extracting data from databases using Application Programming Interfaces (APIs). Regardless of how and where data is stored, the initial step in any data management process involves loading it into your preferred working tool.

Relational databases, such as RMySQL, and web-based databases, like REDCap, have gained popularity for efficiently and cost-effectively managing small to medium-sized datasets. In this blog, I’ll guide you through the essential steps to access and utilize data stored in these platforms using the R statistical language. I will provide practical examples to demonstrate:

  1. Establishing an efficient connection between R and Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMS).

  2. Querying data housed in any RDBMS directly from within R/RStudio.

  3. Connecting to and querying data from a Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) database.

  4. Best practices for securing your API while collaborating on projects.

Please note that this blog is a work in progress. In the meantime, you can access the workshop slides for reference here and the youtube link should be resourceful since this was a live coding exercise.

item.title: Automating Clinical Data Management
item.description:
Using REDCap, RStudio Server and Shiny Server

Introduction

Data management in multi-centre cohort studies is challenging, especially when the sites are spread across different countries and have varying technical and staffing capacity. Checking data quality, resolving data discrepancies quickly and producing progress reports all need to be accurate, systematic and timely.

The Childhood Acute Illness and Nutrition Network (CHAIN) is a multi-centre cohort study that recruited children from nine hospitals in Africa and South Asia. The study collected highly detailed data across many biological and social domains, captured in Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap), a web-based, metadata-driven data capture system.

In this post, I describe how we used REDCap together with the open-source R software to automate the data management workflow for CHAIN.

The problem

The CHAIN database is large, with roughly 4,000 records and 2,000 variables. Extracting it by hand took considerable time, and every round of cleaning and reporting started with that same slow export. Sites also depended on the central coordination team to send them their outstanding data queries and progress updates, which slowed down how quickly issues were resolved.

We needed a setup where:

  • data were extracted and processed automatically, on a schedule
  • each site could see its own data queries and progress without waiting for the central team
  • access was secure and limited to study staff

How the system works

We built the workflow from three components running in a single server environment: REDCap as the central database, RStudio Server for data extraction and processing, and Shiny Server for the web dashboard.

1. Automated data extraction from REDCap

REDCap provides an Application Programming Interface (API) that lets you export records programmatically. From within RStudio Server, we used the {redcapAPI} package to pull the data directly from the CHAIN REDCap project, so nobody had to download exports manually.

The examples below are simplified versions of the approach, using placeholder field names rather than the actual CHAIN variables. A connection needs the URL of your REDCap API and a project API token. Keep the token out of your scripts, for example in an .Renviron file on the server:

library(redcapAPI)

# REDCAP_API_TOKEN is set in ~/.Renviron, never in the script itself
rcon <- redcapConnection(
  url   = "https://redcap.example.org/api/",
  token = Sys.getenv("REDCAP_API_TOKEN")
)

# export all records, with values converted to their REDCap field types
records  <- exportRecordsTyped(rcon)

# the data dictionary is useful for building checks from field metadata
metadata <- exportMetaData(rcon)

2. Processing and cleaning in RStudio Server

A processing script (Processing.R) takes the extracted data and runs the custom data cleaning checks and summary calculations. Its outputs include the data query listings for each site and the summaries that feed the progress reports.

Each check returns the records that fail it, with a message describing the query, so the results from all checks can be stacked into one query listing:

library(dplyr)

# example checks: a missing required field and an out-of-range value
missing_weight <- records |>
  filter(is.na(weight_kg)) |>
  transmute(site, record_id, query = "Weight is missing")

implausible_muac <- records |>
  filter(muac_cm < 5 | muac_cm > 25) |>
  transmute(site, record_id, query = "MUAC outside 5-25 cm")

queries <- bind_rows(missing_weight, implausible_muac)

# recruitment summary per site for the progress reports
recruitment <- records |>
  count(site, name = "enrolled")

To make this hands-off, we scheduled the script with the {cronR} package, which sets up cron jobs from R. The extraction and processing then ran automatically at set intervals. Scheduling takes two calls, run once on the server:

library(cronR)

# build the command that runs Processing.R and writes a log next to it
cmd <- cron_rscript("/home/datamanager/chain/Processing.R")

# run it every day at 2 AM
cron_add(cmd, frequency = "daily", at = "2AM",
         id = "chain_processing",
         description = "Extract CHAIN data from REDCap and refresh dashboards")

cron_ls()                         # list scheduled jobs
# cron_rm(id = "chain_processing") # remove the job

3. Exporting results to the Shiny apps

At the end of each run, the processed data are exported into the folders of the Shiny applications. Because the apps read from these folders, the dashboard always shows the results of the most recent run without anyone redeploying anything.

The last lines of Processing.R save the outputs where the apps expect them:

app_dir <- "/srv/shiny-server/chain-dashboard/data"

saveRDS(queries,     file.path(app_dir, "queries.rds"))
saveRDS(recruitment, file.path(app_dir, "recruitment.rds"))

Inside the Shiny app, reading the files in the server function means they are loaded each time a user opens the dashboard, so every session picks up the latest run:

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  queries <- readRDS("data/queries.rds")
  # ... outputs built from queries
}

4. A secure web dashboard for site teams

The Shiny apps run within Shiny Server and together make up an interactive web dashboard. Study staff at the nine sites log in with authenticated credentials, and each site team can see:

  • listings of site-specific data queries to resolve
  • customised progress reports
  • real-time recruitment progress against targets

What changed

With the automation in place, extracting and processing the data became seamless instead of a time-consuming manual step.

  • Less reliance on the central team. Sites follow up on their own data queries on the dashboard instead of waiting for query lists to be sent to them.
  • Better recruitment planning. Real-time progress information helps sites plan recruitment against their targets.
  • Better communication and data quality. Overall, communication with sites improved, and so did data quality, which is paramount to the success of a large cohort study.

Conclusion

Our experience with CHAIN showed that combining REDCap and R makes data management for a large multi-site study efficient. The same setup also gives real-time, interactive monitoring of a wide range of data quality checks, which helps ensure high-quality and reliable study data.

Everything in this workflow is open source, so it can be adapted by other studies that already use REDCap, including those with limited resources.
